articles.title: Cloudflare Reports 18.2 Million Network-Layer DDoS Attacks in Q3, Up 38%
articles.context: Threat actors are launching about 8,226 network-layer distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks per hour, Cloudflare revealed Thursday
articles.full_text:
Threat actors are launching about 8,226 network-layer distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks per hour, Cloudflare revealed Thursday.

The web infrastructure and security company said it autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer (L3) DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests in the third quarter of 2026. That amounts to 197,400 attacks per day, or one attack every 0.44 seconds.

In comparison, a total of 13.2 million and 10.0 million L3 DDoS attacks were recorded in Q2 and Q1 2026, respectively. The increase has been linked to DDoS-for-hire booter or stresser services that are responsible for hundreds of thousands of attacks.

"Short-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%," the Cloudforce One threat intelligence team said in its quarterly DDoS Threat Report shared with The Hacker News.

An interesting trend is the decline of hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps by 69% from the previous quarter – going from 805 attacks in Q2 to 251 in Q3 – likely as a result of law enforcement actions against AISURU, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad earlier this March.

Still, the threat remains far from completely neutralized, given the emergence of new variants like Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot, Cloudflare warned.

Another notable shift is the decline in Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (CLDAP) floods, while DNS amplification jumped 215% to account for 3.43% of all network-layer attacks.

The most targeted industries include media, production, and publishing; information technology and services; gambling and casinos; computer software; and telecommunications providers.

The U.S., China, Indonesia, the U.K., and Türkiye emerged as the most attacked countries during the time period, with Canada and Israel entering the top 10 ranking, fueled by attacks targeting Canada's retail, telecommunications, and marketing sectors.

articles.title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
articles.context: While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar, TÜRKTRUST, and TrustWave), access to their keys has always been contained...
articles.full_text:
On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems.

Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar, TÜRKTRUST, and TrustWave), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by anyone from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independently recover these same signing keys and create certificates for any domain that an unpatched client not enforcing Certificate Transparency would accept.

eMudhra announced they’re exiting the public CA business and have claimed a mistake in a key generation script, but have not yet shared the script. They signed a certificate revocation list (CRL) with what might’ve been a correctly generated key, and subsequently corrected it to be signed with the weak key.

How did that come to be and why didn’t that set off alarms? Much has to be cleared up, including the role of the auditors and cross signers. This blog proposes the fixes and next steps for organizations to ensure they are secure.

Patching Cloudflare

Our primary concern remains the security impact on Cloudflare, our customers, and the Internet as a whole. At the time of writing, all high priority Cloudflare systems have been patched. A small number of confirmed low impact tickets is being worked on.

We started patching high-impact systems immediately on October 19. These included customer origin-facing proxies using Pingora, responsible for most of our outbound connections. These were patched in hours to reject the vulnerable eMudhra keys. At the same time, we started an AI-assisted analysis of our source code to find all other systems that trust these weak keys. Within four hours we had a full analysis. We assigned a ticket with preliminary analysis for each system, and asked the team to confirm and/or adjust the analysis before the end of the day. Where high impact was identified, we asked to patch immediately, and for the lower impact, remediation was due at the end of last week.

Has Cloudflare seen exploitation across its network?

To track whenever a customer’s server (or attacker) presents a certificate signed by eMudhra’s weak keys, we added logging to Pingora. As this outbound service accounts for the vast majority of outgoing TLS connections from a Cloudflare machine, any attacker attempting to snoop using the eMudhra keys would trigger this logging. The logging finished rolling out October 21.

At the time of writing, a week later, we’ve seen about 22,000 attempted handshakes with the weak eMudhra keys. Two-thirds of the attempts were fetches of test sites such as emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (which we mentioned in the developer guidance in our earlier post). Almost all of the remaining third went to origins who appeared to set up a certificate for themselves using the weak intermediate. Every handshake configured to verify the certificate was refused, as we already patched.

About 160 of these handshakes stood out: the certificates’ Subject Alternative Names (SANs) were naming other organizations’ domains, unrelated to the Server Name Indication (SNI) requested in the handshake. Some of those names were domains related to consumer IoT devices. We noticed as well that those forged certificates were made after the keys leaked and some were valid for over two years, longer than any public CA may issue. However, these certificates looked like the servers' own default certificates rather than part of an attempt to intercept our connections. They named domains other than the ones being connected to, so they would have failed hostname verification anyway. And in several cases, a server presented the same certificate to connections from many of our locations, which means it came from the server itself rather than from something on a single network path.

Thus while there is no evidence of the weak keys being used to intercept Cloudflare's connections so far, these keys appear to have been used to forge certificates within hours of the weakness becoming public: one of the forged certificates we saw was dated October 20 at 18:19 UTC, less than an hour after Mozilla's bug report was made public. This does not exclude carefully targeted interception. For that we have to rely on the usual indirect signals of system compromise — and so far, we have not seen any such signals.

How many visitors are still vulnerable?

So much about patching Cloudflare, but what about our visitors? We cannot directly test whether a visitor still trusts the weak keys without breaking connections, so we have to do something more indirect. For that we used our challenge pages:

We rolled out an update to send out two probe connections on a fraction of challenge pages: one probe to ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and one to ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com. Initially we installed an eMudhra signed certificate on ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and a regularly signed certificate on ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com as control. Then we record whether these probes succeeded. This allows us to see if visitors that are served a challenge page still trust the weak eMudhra keys.

What did we find? With 50 million probes over the last week, we see this:

Big caveat upfront: by design the traffic to these challenge pages is highly skewed. There are many (unconfirmed) bots in there. Also, only clients that execute JavaScript (like browsers) will send probes.

The jump in the data is due to the following changes—all times are UTC:

October 23 15:30, we changed our control endpoint to also serve an eMudhra certificate, but this time without signed certificate timestamps (SCTs). There were some differences in acceptance, but not large. We could’ve added a new endpoint, but that would’ve required a slow release of our challenge platform. Changing the endpoint was easier.

October 23 16:30, our challenge platform rolled back to a previous version because of an unrelated issue. The probes returned October 27 at 10:00.

October 27 16:37, we noticed we did not send the G3 cross-sign, which not all clients knew about, and added it to both endpoints. We removed SCTs from both.

October 27 16:49, we switched ca2 to chain up to the AAA Certificate Services root.

October 27 18:18, we ramped up probes to be included from 1% to 10% of all challenge pages served on non-paying customer zones.

With those caveats out of the way: what do we notice? Up-to-date modern browsers are mostly patched, but bots and old browsers are not. Also embedded browsers, like Android WebView, lag behind patching with 30–40% still accepting. Over the first weekend (with the monitoring gap), we see clear evidence of patching, but afterwards we see little movement.

On October 29 around 18:00 UTC, we released a detection that caught a large influx of bot traffic identifying as Chrome 150-154 on macOS. This can look like patching in the top graph, but it is actually a change in traffic classification: the same user agents show a corresponding increase in acceptance among traffic with bot signals detected in the bottom graph.

Chrome 150-154 on Linux is the notable exception: its acceptance continues to decline, consistent with further patching in that cohort. Given the bot-heavy and changing traffic mix, that evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Otherwise, we still see little movement.

Breaking down by network (ASN) we see:

Across the large networks, more than half of probes still accept the compromised chain, both among traffic with no bot signals detected (top graph) and traffic with bot signals detected (bottom graph). Over the weekend we saw some patching, but afterwards the trend has been flat.

The big caveat still holds: traffic is skewed by (unconfirmed) bots. But bots are also just software that need security updates. And if they’re in any way representative of overall software updates, then the picture is quite dire indeed.

What can you do?

Patch! Dennis Jackson has a great crowdsourced website with instructions. Especially if you’re a developer on macOS, you want to follow these instructions. If you’re a Cloudflare customer, check out last week’s blog post on what needs to be done on your end when using certain products like WARP or Tunnel.

Looking ahead

At Cloudflare, we have a quick-revocation mechanism in place in some products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys. As vulnerabilities are discovered at a faster pace than ever, it is vital that they can be addressed quickly and effectively.

articles.title: In Other News: Anthropic Breach Dispute, UEFI Flaw Hits Most Servers, Cloudflare AI Data Leak
articles.context: This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help...
articles.full_text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.

This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.

Here are this week’s highlights:

Iran suspected in US military freezer hacks

US officials suspect Iran-linked hackers caused freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at around six military base commissaries starting in late August, Nextgov reports, citing people familiar with the matter. At Fort Huachuca in Arizona, a freezer entered defrost mode and heated its contents, and Cyber Command and Defense Department law enforcement units are investigating with French authorities, after hackers overrode refrigeration controls at some 350 French establishments earlier this month.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Most servers rely on UEFI code hit by critical boot flaw

A critical 16-year-old buffer overflow (CVE-2026-97631) in TianoCore EDK II, open source code that most of the world’s server vendors and data centers use through firmware suppliers such as AMI, Insyde and Phoenix, means the flaw affects most servers worldwide, Ars Technica reports. An attacker with local network access can send an oversized ICMP error message to a machine while it boots over the network (PXE) to hang the process or, if the target’s firmware build is known, run code at the highest privilege level before defenses such as Secure Boot take effect. Only machines that use network boot are exposed, and the flaw, found by Anthropic and Google researchers, became public months ahead of a planned January disclosure after AMI published a code fix, leaving organizations to seek firmware updates from their vendors.

Anthropic disputes scope of ex-DOGE startup’s AI-led intrusion

Cathedral, a cybersecurity startup founded by former DOGE staffers, says its AI agents found ways into Anthropic’s internal systems in less than 12 hours by abusing weaknesses in third-party business software, reaching meeting transcripts, salary and job offer data, and Slack discussions about the company’s most advanced models, according to a draft report reviewed by the Washington Post (paywalled). Anthropic, which received the findings through its bug bounty program, says only a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems was reached, that it cut off the startup’s access the same day, and that Claude conversations, source code and model weights were not affected. It also accuses Cathedral of breaking the bounty program’s rules by not disclosing all of its activity.

Midterm spending disclosures stall after FEC intrusion attempt

The US Federal Election Commission took its electronic filing system offline after someone attempted to breach its systems, according to an internal FEC email seen by Reuters, leaving political groups unable to submit campaign finance reports a week before the November 3 midterm elections. The outage blocked the 24-hour and 48-hour reports that track last-minute spending on specific races, although past filings remained searchable. The system was restored on October 28.

Hackers obtain national ID numbers, card PINs in University of Copenhagen breach

The University of Copenhagen says hackers who gained access to one of its test environments obtained personal data on about 525,000 current and former members of the university community, including names, phone numbers and personal email addresses, along with national identity (CPR) numbers for many of them. The attack was detected on October 20 and contained, but the PIN codes for the ID cards of roughly 20,000 staff and students were also compromised and have since been reissued. The university says it does not yet know who is behind the attack or what the motive was.

ENGIE data breach traced to tool used by sales partners

French energy giant ENGIE says attackers stole customer data after gaining access to a tool its partners use for customer prospecting and marketing energy offers, but that its own internal IT systems were not compromised. The incident is limited to customers in France, and notification letters say the stolen data includes names, contact details, customer IDs, contract numbers and energy supply point identifiers, but no banking information. ENGIE has not said how many customers are affected, and no group has claimed the attack.

Fake ChatGPT and Claude bots probe sites for leaked secrets

Cequence has tracked a single threat actor that rotates through about 32 AI bot identities (including crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Perplexity) while scanning websites for files that commonly hold secrets, such as .env files, cloud credentials and private SSH keys. Running from a major cloud provider since at least late September, the scanner used more than 300 IP addresses in a single day and, on one day in October, reached 48% of the Cequence-protected organizations that saw any AI bot traffic. Cequence warns that a bot’s self-declared identity can’t be trusted, noting that the impersonator accounted for more than 80% of traffic labeled as AI bot traffic at some organizations.

Cloudflare and SGLang fix cross-tenant data leak in AI inference

Cloudflare says that between August 27 and September 9, 155 responses from the GLM 5.3 model on its Workers AI platform contained data from other customers’ recent requests to the same model, all involving prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. The leak resulted from a configuration mismatch that left the model’s KV cache smaller than its advertised context window, combined with a bug in the SGLang inference engine that allowed over-length requests to read cache data left behind by earlier sessions. Cloudflare fixed the issue after Knostic researcher Gadi Evron reported it via HackerOne, found no evidence of deliberate exploitation, and recommends that SGLang operators update to version 0.5.22 or later.

Defense worker, Russian money movers targeted over North Korean IT scheme

John Allen Kurrle Jr., 62, a defense contractor employee with a Top Secret clearance, has pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy for aiding a North Korean remote IT worker scheme by letting foreign individuals use his identity (and that of a third person) to apply for remote jobs and hosting victim companies’ laptops at his home. The applications led to nine job offers from US companies, and Kurrle faces up to 20 years in prison. Separately, OFAC sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity supporting North Korea’s IT worker schemes, including two Russians who allegedly converted the workers’ crypto earnings into cash, two North Koreans who managed Russia-based IT worker groups, and the Russia-based First Financial and Technical Development Center (FFTDC), which deploys North Korean IT workers abroad.

Rockwell aims SecureOT at OEMs facing CRA and machinery rules

Rockwell Automation has added OEM-focused capabilities to its SecureOT offering to help machine builders prepare for cybersecurity requirements under the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and Machinery Regulation. Built on the SecureOT Platform, the additions include machine-level inventories of hardware, software and firmware, vulnerability identification, continuous monitoring for newly disclosed flaws after deployment, and exportable compliance reports for customers and auditors. Rockwell is also offering assessments and advisory services to help OEMs find gaps, set up governance processes, and align with standards such as IEC 62443.

AI moves deeper into ransomware, C2 malware and grey-market tooling

Sophos says the Gold Ogre group behind Aur0ra ransomware has used AI extensively, with agents orchestrated through Cursor handling network discovery, credential attacks and lateral movement with limited human involvement, after the operators bypassed guardrails by framing the intrusions as authorized red team work. Cisco Talos has detailed NIK C2, a new AI-integrated command-and-control framework whose Windows implant can steal credentials, stream keystrokes and deploy screen-locking ransomware. Symantec and Carbon Black, meanwhile, warn of a grey-market relay service, seen at a dozen organizations mostly in mainland China, that installs the genuine Codex and Claude Code CLIs but reconfigures them to route all requests through third-party servers with sandboxing disabled.

articles.title: Introducing the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge
articles.context: We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and...
articles.full_text:
Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First, eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised, creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came php2shell: serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web.

Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and introduced a new feature called full transaction detection.

As always in situations like this, these new capabilities were made available on all plans, including Free.

Put our WAF to the test

Protecting systems from vulnerabilities like these is always an ongoing process, not a one-time event. The widespread adoption of AI allows attackers to discover new vectors with unprecedented speed and efficiency, so collecting real-world data to test our assumptions and strengthen defenses is essential.

That’s why today we're launching the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge, run through our Bug Bounty program. We've put a deliberately vulnerable PHP installation behind our WAF, and we're inviting security researchers on HackerOne to try to bypass the protections and capture a flag.

How this Capture the Flag (CTF) works

We are keeping this simple. The challenge focuses on CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the two PHP vulnerabilities behind php2shell. The target runs stock PHP 8.5.11 (with standard PHP extensions), Apache 2 (via mod_php), and an empty index.php inside a Cloudflare Container, with our default WAF protection rules for these vulnerabilities enabled in front of it. Inside the sandbox is a file called /flag.

The sandbox is reset every few minutes, including the flag file.

Your mission, should you choose to accept it: bypass the WAF protections, exploit the PHP sandbox, and recover the contents of /flag. You can use your own research tools. The challenge page has the environment details, scope, and flag verification form.

Challenge requirements

This limited-time challenge is run via Cloudflare's Bug Bounty program on HackerOne. All aspects of this challenge are subject to HackerOne terms and the Cloudflare HackerOne program rules the (“Bounty Terms”). If you find an eligible bypass, you must follow these requirements in order to claim the bounty:

All participants must sign up for a HackerOne account and review and agree to the Bounty Terms before participating in the CTF.

Demonstrate attacker-controlled PHP code or command execution inside the sandbox through an authorized POST request.

Use that remote code execution (RCE) to recover the current contents of /flag, then successfully verify the flag through the CTF user interface (UI). Verify promptly before a reset; retain the successful result for later review.

Submit a private report to Cloudflare on HackerOne. Include PHP CTF in the title and provide:

The endpoint, complete payload, and request sequence, preserving relevant headers, encoding, and body bytes.

Raw request/response captures or a readable proof of concept sufficient to reproduce the full chain.

An explanation of the WAF bypass, executed code or command, and how that execution recovered /flag.

The attempt ID, successful UI verification result, and exploit/verification UTC timestamps. Include the flag privately if needed for verification.

What makes the method or payload materially distinct, and related submissions you know about.

UI verification does not submit a HackerOne report or establish reporting priority. File disclosure without RCE, RCE without successful flag recovery and UI verification, local-only exploits, rediscovery of the known PHP vulnerabilities, and WAF detection differences or partial chains without the full objective are not eligible.

Awards require a materially distinct Firewall (WAF) bypass method, even for the same PHP CVE. Reports using the same Firewall-bypass mechanism are duplicates, regardless of differences in the PHP exploit, payload, RCE technique, or flag-recovery method. New flags, resets, attempt IDs, or cosmetic changes—including equivalent encodings—do not qualify as unique. Equivalent submissions are duplicates even if unfixed; only the first complete, reproducible HackerOne report is considered. Cloudflare makes final duplicate and reward decisions.

We record attempted metadata and request payloads to help analyze reports, so please use test data only. Do not send credentials, personal information, or anything else you would not want included in a research record. Read Cloudflare’s privacy notice before testing.

Testing is authorized only against the challenge hostname's WAF-protected /php/* endpoints (POST method only). Other Cloudflare services, direct access to the underlying infrastructure, the upstream PHP project, and third-party systems are out of scope. No denial of service, high-volume scanning, persistence, social engineering, or attacks on other participants. If you get a 429 or 503, back off.

In the event of any conflict between this blog post and the Bounty Terms, the Bounty Terms shall prevail.

Cloudflare reserves the right to suspend or terminate this challenge at any time. Once the competition is removed from HackerOne, it is officially terminated, so please refer to the Cloudflare HackerOne page for the most up-to-date information on whether this challenge remains open.

Not a substitute for patching

Our WAF protects you, but it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Response blocking can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. If you run PHP, follow the latest PHP security advisories and apply the relevant updates.

Last week was a reminder that helping build a better Internet often takes many people—researchers, maintainers, and teams across the industry—doing difficult, urgent work together.

We hope this challenge gives everyone a useful way to join in. Head over to php-rce.cloudflare.app if you want to participate: the flag is there, and we'd like to know if you can get it.

articles.title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
articles.context: We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation
articles.full_text:
On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected.

Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.

After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs.

What happened

GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day.

This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.

The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions.

Immediate remediation

After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it:

To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised.

To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe. Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as #38704, which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang main in #36988, merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged #38935, which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach.

We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model.

Background: how we serve GLM 5.3

Workers AI runs GLM 5.3 with SGLang in a disaggregated configuration: a pool of prefill GPUs processes the prompt and produces the model's KV cache for it, then hands that cache over remote direct memory access (RDMA), via Mooncake, to a pool of decode GPUs that generate the response. We have written about this architecture before in our posts on high-performance LLMs and smaller, faster, safer models.

The KV cache in GPU memory is a shared pool of fixed-size pages. Each request is assigned pages when it is admitted and releases them when it finishes. Pages are not currently zeroed between requests; the next request that gets a page simply overwrites it. This approach is common among inference engines and is necessary to achieve the best performance, but it means that the inference engine is responsible for tracking ownership of these memory pages. KV cache page ownership and lifetime tracking has to deal with not just shared ownership within a node (KV cache offload and token generation both access the memory with different lifetimes), but also ownership that is technically shared with the remote prefill node (which holds a simultaneous mutable reference to the page).

Furthermore, the size of this pool is not a configuration value. SGLang sizes it at startup from whatever GPU memory remains after loading the model weights. The model's advertised context length is a separate configuration value. Nothing forces the two to agree, and it is our job to check that they do.

Issue one: misconfiguration

On our GLM 5.3 prefill nodes with our configuration, the pool came to 681,280 tokens while the model's context length is 1,048,576 tokens. The selected KV pool size is printed by SGLang in logs during startup and exposed as a metric. We were aware of this size mismatch; however, during pre-launch testing we observed successful HTTP status codes and a streaming body with no error frames during benchmarking. We assumed that the engine was capable of gracefully handling the difference between the KV cache pool and requested context window via streaming or some other mechanism.

This was one critical gap in our testing: we only validated HTTP response codes and engine performance at long contexts, without validating model output and coherence. We now check KV pool size against context length directly, from the running engine, before any disaggregated deployment change ships, rather than inferring it from response codes.

Issue two: SGLang bug

In v0.5.21, the SGLang team has now addressed this bug in how it was handling prompts longer than the KV pool size. Here’s what was happening before.

When a prompt arrived that was longer than the KV pool could hold, SGLang's scheduler rejected it. The rejection path (Req.set_finish_with_abort) recorded the error to be returned to the client and swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder so that the request could drain through the normal batch machinery without allocating real memory. On a single-node deployment this worked: the placeholder ran, the batch finished, and the client received an error.

In disaggregated mode such as we operate, the admission queues on both prefill and decode checked whether a request was finished, not whether it was rejected. A rejected request reported itself as live. So:

Bootstrap. The router told the decode node the prompt length (8 pages in the diagram). Decode reserved 8 KV pages for the request.

Prefill admission. The prefill admission queue admitted any request where req.finished() was False. A rejected request stored its rejection in to_finish, not finished_reason, so finished() still returned False. The rejected request was admitted.

Prefill forward pass. Rejection had already replaced the prompt with a one-token placeholder. Prefill ran a trivial forward pass on that one token.

KV transfer. Prefill sent one page of KV to decode and signaled that the transfer was complete.

Decode admission. Decode's admission queue had the same finished() check, so it accepted the handoff.

Decode attention. Decode started generating and attention read all 8 reserved pages. Only page P0 had been written by this request. Pages P1 to P7 still held what earlier requests left in them: other users' prompts and partial generations.

Response. The client got HTTP 200 instead of HTTP 400. prompt_tokens matched the long prompt and the reply was coherent. It arrived faster than an 8-page prefill should take, and it contained content from other users' KV pages.

Every request over the threshold behaved this way. This bug had been reported to SGLang by another user as issue #30233 on July 6, 2026, which Cloudflare noticed while investigating this incident. We had been flagging these types of issues with SGLang since v0.5.10 and this security incident sped up work that Cloudflare had already started in collaboration with the SGLang team. The patch for this issue was released in SGLang v0.5.20, with follow-ups in v0.5.21 and v0.5.22, and is available for all other operators dependent on SGLang to use. We highly recommend all operators update SGLang dependencies to v0.5.22 or later. For more details on specific PRs, read on below.

GLM 5.3 was the only model affected by this bug. Every other disaggregated deployment on Workers AI has KV pools larger than its context length on both prefill and decode, so no request could reach the rejection path. We have applied the engine fix and the hardening described below to every model we serve with SGLang, and our deployment checks require them for every new deployment.

Timeline

All times UTC.

When

What

Aug 27, 2026

Sep 8, 2026 - 23:11

Sep 9, 2026 - 13:22

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:00

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:35

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:52

SGLang v0.5.21 released.

SGLang v0.5.22 released.

Coordinated publication with the researcher and RadixArk.

Ongoing hardening effort

This bug belongs to a class of KV cache memory-safety bugs that Cloudflare has been working to address for several months. In each case, a page is freed, reused, or read while something else still has a claim on it. We see two common causes.

The first is page lifetime within a single node. Several tasks on a decode node can hold the same page at once: token generation, offload to host memory, the KV transfer receiver, and the abort and error paths. If one of them frees the page while another is still using it, a new request can be given that page while it is still being read or written. Our earlier fixes for decode offload (#24226, #30899) and double release on grammar errors (#30937) were of this kind.

The second is a race across nodes. When a request is aborted while prefill is still writing its KV cache to decode over RDMA, the writes already sent cannot be recalled. If decode frees those pages right away, those pages can be given to another request, and the late writes land in that request's KV cache. Cloudflare has contributed to the effort to fix this race through proposed fixes (#31357, #38961) and a reproduction script (#32564). In both cases the result is corrupted output, or one user's data in another user's response, with no error raised. The bug in this incident was different: a rejected request went through the handoff every time, rather than by a timing accident. But it had the same result: decode reading pages this request never wrote. None of these covered the failure in this incident in which prefill rejected the request, and decode never learned of it.

Since the incident, we have:

Extended deferred release to hold prefill's source pages as well, and to cover every failure type, not just aborts. We proposed it upstream as #38961, which was superseded by #40645, #41402, and #41404.

Deployed bounded Mooncake transfer batches (#32758, from the SGLang community), so no single transfer call can outlast the release timeout.

Changed our load balancer so a client disconnect no longer aborts a request mid-transfer. It holds the prefill connection until prefill finishes and the decode connection until the first token, then closes both.

Added a check to every disaggregated deployment change: KV pool size measured against context length, deferred release on both roles, transfer batch bounds inside the release timeout, and all required patches applied.

All of these changes were released to our disaggregated production deployments.

Working with the SGLang team

We met with the SGLang maintainers at RadixArk on September 10, the day after the incident. We agreed that RadixArk would investigate the race conditions we had reported, upstream the integrity-checking idea, and build reproduction tests for this class of bug.

The following have landed on SGLang main to address this incident and related KV cache race conditions, and all but one are included in v0.5.22. Operators running disaggregated SGLang should update to v0.5.22 or backport these patches as needed.

Category

These follow-ups are still works in progress:

#39729 Additional cleanup for --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum. Merged, awaiting release.

Zero KV pages on release, draft proposal: #46435

Extend KV checksum validation from the prefill-to-decode handoff to every decode step (see Integrity by construction, below)

Broader KV Canary and KV Checksum model and feature support

What we recommend to other operators

If you run SGLang in disaggregated prefill/decode mode, we recommend the following:

Measure your KV pool and compare it to your context length, on every prefill and decode node, from the engine's startup log, after every change to weights, quantization, parallelism, or memory fraction. If the pool is smaller, lower the context length to fit. Do not rely on a proxy to enforce the limit, and do not assume the engine will reject what does not fit. This is the check we did not enforce.

Upgrade to a build that includes #36988 and #38935 (v0.5.22 or later), so an over-length request is rejected before handoff regardless of pool size. This is the engine-side fix, and it is the backstop for the day your check in step one is wrong.

Run with deferred KV release on both roles (default after #41023), and bound your Mooncake transfer batches so a single timed-out call cannot leave an unbounded tail of writes.

Turn on corruption detection where your model supports it. --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum and --kv-canary do not yet cover every model architecture. Check your logs to confirm requests are being verified. We are working with the SGLang team to extend both checks to more architectures, including GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.

Ensure your proxy is not generating unnecessary aborts. Configure your load balancer to allow requests to proceed up to the first token, so that you do not trigger an abort that requires cross-node coordination.

Longer term

Integrity by construction

Configuration checks and lifecycle fixes reduce the number of ways a page can be misused. They do not make misuse impossible, and this incident is a reminder that the next bug will have a shape we have not seen. The durable answer is for the engine to detect, at read time, that a request is about to attend over a page it does not own, and fail that one request rather than return someone else's data.

We built a prototype of this over the summer and described it in August. Every physical KV page carries a tag that changes when the page is reallocated, each request records the tags it expects, and the mapping is checked before decode reads the cache. In our tests it cost under 1% in throughput and tail latency. We tested it on GLM 5.2 in mid-August, but disabled it shortly afterwards due to reliability issues.

The prototype was also tied to specific attention backends and model architectures, so it could not be a general fix. We are working with the SGLang team to build a production version into the engine that works across every model, rather than maintaining Cloudflare-specific patches. The per-transfer checksum in #39500 is a first step: it validates the handoff from prefill to decode. Page-level tags go further, because they check every read, including reads long after the transfer.

Integrity by mathematical impossibility

RDMA copies data directly from one node’s memory to another’s. It’s vital for the two machines to agree on where the data goes, how large it is, and when it’s finished; any mismatch can cause the receiver to read the wrong data. This bug is an example of a consistency failure in a distributed system, in which the two machines had inconsistent views of the state of that system.

Elsewhere in Cloudflare, we have put effort into proving the safety of distributed systems using formal verification methods. Topaz enables conflict-free IP selection for our authoritative DNS servers. Models of Meerkat’s QuePaxa implementation have demonstrated consistency bugs that were subsequently fixed.

We are now directing our experience in formal methods to KV cache transfer engines. This will start with modeling and proving the safety of an RDMA-based KV cache transfer protocol. The goal is to model our production SGLang’s distributed KV cache system using Mooncake, then track and fix any divergence from the safety properties we want to guarantee. The aim is to prove — as far as possible — that a bug like this cannot occur again. Realistically, we expect gaps in what the provers can tell us, but proving the rest of the system allows us to more closely review and monitor those gaps.

Coordinated disclosure

We are publishing this report as part of a coordinated disclosure. We want to thank the researcher, Gadi Evron, who reported this through our HackerOne program with a clear, reproducible script and gave us time to fix it and to coordinate with the SGLang maintainers before publishing. We also want to thank the SGLang team at RadixArk, who treated this as their problem as well as ours and landed the upstream fixes with urgency.

Read more at the post from the SGLang team.

If you find a security issue in Workers AI, please report it at hackerone.com/cloudflare.

articles.title: Cloudflare Introduces a Faster TypeScript Compiler Written in Rust
articles.context: Cloudflare announced on October 20 that it is bringing tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, into its Oxc toolchain
articles.full_text:
Microsoft’s Go port of TypeScript’s compiler and tooling delivered roughly 10× faster type checking. Now Cloudflare is working on a Rust port of TypeScript’s compiler that promises even faster type checking and lower memory use. The TypeScript team is collaborating on the work, and some of the optimizations are already making their way into the official compiler.

Cloudflare announced on October 20 that it is bringing tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, into its Oxc toolchain. Its VoidZero team is taking on development and maintenance.

The project began with Max Schwenk, head of AI developer experience at Owner.com, a company that makes software for restaurants. Type checking its large TypeScript backend was consuming enough time and memory to make running several coding agents on a laptop impractical. Schwenk used Claude coding agents to build the initial Rust port, then tested and optimized it against the Go compiler before moving the project to Oxc.

For VoidZero, which Cloudflare acquired in June, this extends years of work on JavaScript tools written in Rust. Its projects include the Oxc parser and compiler tools, the Rolldown bundler, the Oxlint linter, and the Oxfmt formatter. A TypeScript compiler fits naturally alongside that work and could supply the type information needed by tools such as Oxlint.

The Oxc team has already begun refactoring tsrs to improve performance, memory usage, and maintainability. Schwenk says the team cut two releases on its first day. Some optimizations discovered in tsrs have also made their way back into the official TypeScript compiler.

The compiler race has moved beyond Microsoft’s Go port

Microsoft announced its native Go port in March 2025, promising roughly a tenfold performance improvement over the JavaScript implementation. Now other teams are porting that implementation again.

Bun introduced bun check on October 10, reporting type checking 3× to 6.4× faster than TypeScript 7.0.2 in its benchmarks. It ports the Go compiler and checks types without emitting JavaScript or providing an editor language server. Theo Browne’s tsc-rs, another Rust port of TypeScript’s compiler, is being merged with tsrs. Vercel Labs has even ported the Go compiler back into TypeScript, then compiled it to native code with scriptc.

AI coding agents have also changed how long a project like this takes. Cloudflare says current models can carry out large-scale ports almost independently in days. Peter Steinberger contrasted that with the time Microsoft spent on its Go port:

tsrs reports faster checks with substantially less memory #

Cloudflare reports that tsrs is up to 8× faster and uses approximately 70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0 with the same number of type checking workers.

The company also addresses the competing benchmark claims directly. Different machine sizes and compiler settings can produce very different results, it says, and it worked with the TypeScript team to compare equivalent configurations. The benchmark tooling and methodology are public.

Those figures describe the matched configuration. By default, tsrs adapts to the machine it runs on, trading some additional memory for faster checking.

tsrs started with a resource problem at Owner.com. Its backend has approximately 37,000 TypeScript files checked as one program. Schwenk reports that a single-threaded check with TypeScript 7.0 took 80 seconds and 19 GiB of memory. Add linting, development servers, and several coding agents, and even well-equipped laptops were running out of room.

Early users are reporting improvements on their own projects. Kevin Kern tried it on an application with approximately 190,000 lines of code, calling the results promising.

When several agents are working in separate worktrees, type checking can eat up CPU and memory several times over. Cutting that overhead makes room to run more agents at once. That’s part of the appeal for Jimmy Lai, who is considering a move to tsrs for the ChatGPT codebase.

The TypeScript team is already bringing improvements upstream #

The speed claims have prompted questions about why Microsoft should keep investing in the Go implementation. But the TypeScript team is actively involved in understanding and applying the improvements.

TypeScript’s Daniel Rosenwasser said on Hacker News that the team has been working with tsrs’s maintainers to understand its performance and which optimizations are safe. The team has even tried its own Rust port.

Rosenwasser said “a lot of the speed does not just come down to language choice.” Some improvements discovered in tsrs are contributing to a faster, leaner TypeScript 7.1, and the team will continue improving the official tools.

Cloudflare’s announcement puts TypeScript 7.1 beta at up to 2.5× faster than 7.0. The headline 8× comparison is against 7.0, so it should not be read as an 8× lead over the latest beta.

The Rust ports also build on Microsoft’s existing compiler architecture and test infrastructure. Schwenk’s approach began by preserving the Go implementation’s algorithms and behavior, using TypeScript’s conformance tests to check the result. The team aims to have tsrs behave exactly like the official TypeScript compiler as it evolves.

WebAssembly makes the Rust port useful in more places #

WebAssembly support is another reason Cloudflare wants a Rust implementation.

Go can compile to Wasm, but its garbage collector comes with it. Rust’s memory management avoids bundling that collector and gives developers more direct control over allocation and interaction with the host. Cloudflare sees that as a better fit for development tools running within constrained environments.

The appeal is a complete validation loop that can run close to the code, including inside a browser or a Cloudflare Worker. An agent could edit files and check the result within a sandboxed development environment. A browser-based tool could check a project locally without sending the type checking job to a separate server.

The @tsrs/wasm package already supports checking in-memory project files in browsers, and the project links to a browser playground. The Wasm build currently runs on one thread, does not support watch mode or LSP, and has a maximum of 4 GiB of linear memory per instance.

Oxc gives tsrs a home for continued maintenance #

A fast port needs to keep up with TypeScript’s next release, and the release after that. Cloudflare’s Oxc team is taking on that ongoing work.

They are working with Browne to combine tsc-rs and tsrs into one package, including support for LSP and content mappers. Browne had already expressed doubts about whether he would maintain his separate rewrite. Combining the projects gives that work a path into a compiler with an established tooling team behind it.

Cloudflare intends to use the process it developed for Vinext to track TypeScript: agents review upstream changes, identify compatibility gaps, run upstream tests, and propose fixes. The team is also exploring using tsrs for type-aware lint rules in Oxlint.

AI can produce a compiler port quickly, but that leaves developers wondering who will maintain it once the initial excitement wears off. Amid what VoidZero's Michael Dong calls “slopforks,” tsrs has an established tooling team committing to ongoing compatibility, working with TypeScript’s maintainers, and contributing improvements back.

The team is still working toward a stable release and ironing out differences from the official TypeScript compiler, including the order in which errors are reported. Its maintainers acknowledge remaining differences, including diagnostic ordering. Developers can try the npm package today:

npm install --save-dev tsrs npx tsrs --noEmit

The tsrs maintainers say the TypeScript team will continue to control the language’s design and direction. Their job is to preserve that behavior in Rust and contribute useful improvements upstream. With new compiler ports arriving this quickly, the commitment to keep aligning that work with the TypeScript team is a substantial part of tsrs’s appeal.

articles.title: Localizing compliance at scale: achieving South Korea’s ISMS certification
articles.context: We document the limits of IP geolocation: it is an estimate rather than an exact science, addresses rotate and change ownership, and it should not be the only signal where the...
articles.full_text:
For ten days, auditors appointed by the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) sat together with us and worked through 80 controls. That is what it took for a company headquartered in the United States, operating a global network serving Korean users, to be certified in South Korea. Cloudflare has now obtained South Korea's Information Security Management System (ISMS) certification under the ISMS-P framework.

For customers in Korea, this is more than a compliance checkbox. It is evidence that Cloudflare's security and privacy program has been examined not only for whether our controls exist, but for how they operate in the context of Korean law, the Korean language, and the particular expectations of Korean regulators.

What a Korean user sees when they sign up

The most visible result of this work is the Cloudflare account sign-up page. In most parts of the world, the line that sits above the sign-up button reads: "By continuing, I agree to Cloudflare's terms, privacy policy, and cookie policy."

A user signing up from South Korea sees something different. The Korean experience is triggered by the country selected at sign-up and by IP geolocation from within South Korea, and it breaks the same agreement into four separately labeled items, each marked required or optional, each linking to its full text, with an option to agree to all of them at once:

모두 동의 (Agree to all)

[필수] 서비스 약관 ([Required] Terms of Service)

[필수] 개인정보 수집 및 이용 ([Required] Collection and use of personal information)

[필수] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 해외 이전 ([Required] Transfer of a limited amount of personal information overseas)

[선택] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 제3자 제공 ([Optional] Sharing a limited amount of personal information with marketing third parties)

The three required items are hard gates. The sign-up button stays disabled until all three are checked, so there is no path through the form that creates an account without an affirmative action on each one. The optional item governs marketing permission only, and leaving it unchecked has no effect on the account creation (it merely opts the user out of receiving marketing communications).

The hard part: sign-up paths that never show a form

Itemizing consent on a form we control is straightforward. The difficulty was the sign-up paths that skip that form entirely.

Globally, you can create a Cloudflare account with Google, Apple, or GitHub. Those flows hand the user to an identity provider and return with an authenticated identity, and they never render our own sign-up form, which is precisely where the four consent items live. There is no step in that handoff where we can present three required items, link each to its full Korean text, and require an affirmative action on each before the account exists. The identity provider's screen is not ours to change.

We could either build a separate post-authentication consent gate for one country, or remove the paths that bypass the gate we already had. We chose the second. Social sign-up is not offered in South Korea, so every account created there goes through Cloudflare’s sign-up form, which enforces the required consents.

The country signal is the same one available to any Cloudflare customer. Cloudflare derives a two-letter country code from the client IP address and exposes it on the request, as the CF-IPCountry header at the origin and as request.cf.country inside a Worker. Reduced to its essentials, the branch is a string comparison:

// Illustrative: the shape of the check, not Cloudflare's own dashboard code. export default { async fetch(request) { // Two-letter country code derived from the client IP. // Same value as the CF-IPCountry request header. // Cloudflare's network populates this on the incoming request, so there is // no geolocation database, lookup service, or extra round trip of our own. const country = request.cf?.country; if (country === "KR") { return renderSignUp({ locale: "ko-KR", consent: "itemized", // four separate items, three of them required socialLogin: false, // no path that skips the consent form }); } return renderSignUp({ locale: "en-US", consent: "combined", socialLogin: true }); }, };

What that does not show is why the country code is not the whole trigger. We document the limits of IP geolocation: it is an estimate rather than an exact science, addresses rotate and change ownership, and it should not be the only signal where the use case is critical to meeting the objectives of a local requirement. A Korean resident traveling abroad, or behind a VPN or a mobile carrier's NAT, may not arrive with a Korean address. So IP-based geolocation decides which form appears by default, but the country a user selects at sign-up overrides that and carries the decision from there. The IP address tells us where a request came from; only the user can tell us where they reside. Keeping those two apart is what makes the consent meaningful rather than presumed.

It is a small feature. It took a country-level product decision, and a change to the account creation path.

What ISMS is and why it matters

ISMS is a detailed, localized certification standard. It covers security policy, access control, authentication and permission management, encryption, incident response, risk management, and disaster recovery, all assessed against how personal data actually moves through an organization's systems, and against Korea's Personal Information Protection Act and its associated regulatory guidelines.

Certification requires an independent audit by an auditor appointed by KISA, a governmental institution affiliated with the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT), followed by review from a special committee. It is valid for three years, with an annual audit required to maintain it.

The ISMS certification is primarily established under Article 47 of Korea's Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc., with the certification criteria and procedure set out in its Enforcement Decree and in the public notification on ISMS certification issued by MSIT.

What the audit examined

Cloudflare is already certified against ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, ISO/IEC 27017, ISO/IEC 27018 and many other globally recognized frameworks. ISMS does not replace any of them. It is a localization of the same principles, layered with Korean regulatory requirements, and that changes what auditors look for and how they look for it.

The controls in scope started with the review of data flows. We presented detailed data flow diagrams showing every path by which employees could access personal information that Cloudflare collects, processes, and stores. The flows themselves are not Korea-specific. What was different was the form the evidence had to take: the auditors were not willing to work from a narrative description of how data moves, they wanted diagrams they could read and interrogate. For each one, they examined every access control layer and tested its effectiveness, across our internal systems, our public-facing websites, event pages, and the Cloudflare dashboard, covering the full lifecycle of a user's data from first interaction through to destruction. Those diagrams are not published here due to confidentiality.

The audit also scrutinized the language and terminology of our consent collection: the exact wording at sign-up, the structure of each notification, and whether the items were presented separately and clearly. That is the kind of detail the ISMS framework is designed to surface.

Why the timeline ran to a year and a half

Part of the answer is how audit cycles work. An ISMS audit covers a single annual period, and all evidence, documentation, and systems must reflect that period. Our preparation ran past one audit year and into the next, which meant retranslating updated policies for the new audit year, re-collecting and reassessing evidence, republishing an updated privacy policy, and absorbing formatting and design changes our marketing and website teams had introduced in the meantime.

What the certificate covers

KISA defines the certified scope as a service boundary rather than as an enumerated list of in-scope products. The Statement of Scope submitted to KISA describes that boundary in three parts:

the organizational and operational perimeter: the Cloudflare entities, teams, and processes that operate the service;

the infrastructure perimeter: the network and platform the certified service runs on;

the information assets and personal information flows that fall inside the boundary under the ISMS control set.

If a customer-consumed Cloudflare product is delivered through that certified service boundary, meaning it runs on the same certified platform, is operated by the same certified teams, and is governed by the same ISMS, it is covered by the certificate. The certificate is held by Cloudflare, Inc.

That is a different shape from the reports most procurement teams work with. A SOC 2 report or an ISO 27001 certificate describes the system it covers and names the services included, so coverage is confirmed by finding the product in that list. The ISMS certificate carries no such list. Coverage follows the delivery path instead, whether or not a product is named anywhere.

What this means for customers

For organizations operating in Korea, this gives legal, security, and procurement teams a local assurance benchmark alongside Cloudflare's broader compliance portfolio. ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 demonstrate a general security posture. ISMS reflects Korea-specific legal and regulatory expectations. That distinction matters in third-party risk reviews and in preparing for a team’s own compliance assessments.

Cloudflare’s entry can be found on KISA's public register of certified organizations, which is the independent, verifiable confirmation to cite in a risk review. Broader privacy and data protection material sits on the Cloudflare Trust Hub.

The question that usually stalls a vendor review of Cloudflare is whether a particular product in use is in scope. The certificate does not answer that by name, because it lists no products. It answers by boundary, meaning that the product is in scope if it is delivered through the certified service.

For multinational teams managing security across regions, the certification confirms that Cloudflare's program has been reviewed against local requirements in one of Asia's most important digital markets, not just designed for global scale.

Building a better Internet, for everyone

ISMS is not a harder certification than the other assurance audits we go through. It is a more nuanced one. It is built around the regulatory needs of one specific region, and it asks for genuine investment in understanding and embedding those needs, rather than mapping them onto a common control framework.

Going through it made Cloudflare more global, not less. It pushed us to think carefully about what it means to serve users in a specific local context, with local language, local consent expectations, and local data protection requirements, and to put that into how the product behaves rather than only into a document.

That is consistent with what we are working toward: helping build a better Internet for everyone, not just in the regions where regulatory requirements are straightforward, but everywhere.

To learn more about Cloudflare's compliance and assurance programs, visit our Trust Hub.

articles.title: Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF
articles.context: ref Signature reference IDs, up to 10 The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability
articles.full_text:
Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester.

These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shell vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper.

Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin returns. A suspicious input followed by a response exposing sensitive information tells a different story from the same input followed by a rejection or an error.

With these new capabilities, customers can use Cloudflare-managed protections or build their own policies combining request and response properties. This extends our always-on application security framework, with detection results available in Security Analytics to support investigation. Our first managed protections using this capability address the recently disclosed php2shell vulnerability.

And the best part? We are making these new capabilities generally available to all Cloudflare customers, including Free plans.

Request inspection is not enough

Cloudflare WAF protects websites and APIs with managed rules, custom rules, and rate limiting. Managed rules provide protection for known attack techniques and vulnerabilities while custom rules let teams create their own policies using parameters such as an IP address, URL path, headers, and request body. These controls operate at the request level to stop exploits or unwanted traffic from reaching the origin.

For many threats, this is the right place to act. However, treating every suspicious request as a confirmed exploit creates a difficult choice. Broad request signatures can catch more potential attacks, but they can also show “false positives”, such as matching legitimate traffic — which then breaks the applications. Deploying only rules that do not trigger false positives reduces that risk, but can leave more room for more ambiguous traffic to reach the server.

The response provides the missing evidence. Cloudflare can now correlate it with the request that produced it, so detections can account for the outcome of the entire HTTP transaction.

As an illustrative example, consider an application that lets users download files. An attacker manipulates the file parameter to request a private configuration file outside the permitted directory:

GET /download?file=../../config/database.ini

Request inspection can recognize this path traversal attempt and block it before it reaches the application. The request alone, however, cannot establish whether the application would expose the file. It might reject the request, ignore the traversal, or return an error. If the request reaches the origin, a response like this provides additional evidence:

200 OK Content-Type: text/plain [database] username=app_service password=EXAMPLE_SECRET

Full transaction detection provides a missing piece: it can correlate the attempted file access with response content characteristic of a private configuration file. Configuration-like text can legitimately appear in documentation or example downloads; combining it with a traversal attempt provides stronger evidence of sensitive data exposure than either signal alone. A response rule can then replace the origin response with a Cloudflare WAF block page and HTTP 403 before it reaches the requester, effectively blocking the exploit by preventing sensitive information from reaching the attacker.

Detection and mitigation are separate by design

Full transaction detection extends the always-on detection framework we introduced earlier this year. Detections analyze traffic and attach metadata to the request and response, rules then decide what to do with those results.

Separating those jobs gives customers visibility before they design a policy. Security teams can inspect detections in their own traffic, understand which endpoints and signatures are involved, and choose the response that fits their application. Similar to the approach for the request-based Attack Signature Detection, the outcome of the detections are stored in fields that can be accessed in the response custom rules or used in managed detections to block traffic.

Mirroring the request detection fields, the following new fields are added to our platform:

Field

Description

cf.waf.signature.response.confidence

Confidence values associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.categories

Categories associated with matching signatures

cf.waf.signature.response.ref

Signature reference IDs, up to 10

The first full transaction detections focus on exploit confirmation for high profile vulnerability. It correlates suspicious input with response signals that indicate an exploit may have succeeded.

We will expand coverage over time by supporting other use cases, including detecting data exposure and exfiltration signals. This is important for the Internet beyond any one application: defenses can distinguish probing from evidence of impact, while detection of exposed data and services can reach customers that do not have a dedicated security team tuning every WAF rule.

Create rules on the response

Detecting evidence of exploitation is most useful if you can act on it in real time. Response custom rules turn full transaction detections into inline protection by blocking a matching origin response before it reaches the requester, although it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin.

Security teams can now combine request and response properties with detection results to decide which responses to block. When a blocking rule matches, Cloudflare replaces the origin response with a WAF block page or a custom response.

Response phase controls are available in the Cloudflare dashboard at the bottom of the Security > Security Rules page, with both managed protections and custom rules.

We have released both managed and custom rules to all plans, including Free plans. Over time, we will follow the same approach we use for request detections, where managed detections for free plans focus on high-profile vulnerabilities, while paying customers get a richer catalog of detections.

Managed detections

All customers get the protection of the full array of transaction detections through the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default ruleset, which is designed for a simple one-click deploy and simplified configurability. When a signature matches, the managed detection will block the response and return a standard WAF block page.

You can edit the Cloudflare Managed Response Firewall Default scope to run detections only on a portion of their applications, for example by excluding or restricting the detection to a specific path. Paying customers can use detection fields in custom response rules to create more tailored policies.

Custom rules

Custom response rules are designed to give customers full control of the rule logic. A useful rule can stop an administration interface from being exposed when an authentication gateway has not marked the request as internal. For example:

http.request.uri.path starts_with "/admin" and not http.request.headers["x-internal-user"][0] eq "true" and http.response.code eq 200 and http.response.headers["content-type"][0] contains "text/html"

This blocks only when an unauthenticated request targets `/admin` and the origin actually returns a successful HTML administration page. It does not block ordinary authentication failures, redirects, or non-administration traffic.

All customers can create up to three custom response rules supporting Log and Block actions. The fields and functions available in response to custom rules mirrors what your plan gives you access to in request custom rules already. Creating rules on the response body is not yet available.

Following the Attack Signature Detection approach, paying customers also have access to the outcome of attack detections through the cf.waf.signature.response.* fields listed above. These fields can be combined with other parameters (such as a hostname, URL path, source IP, request header) to enable protection on a single path, or limit the policy to application-specific context. We are currently rolling out the response fields to all our accounts. If you don’t have access to them yet, please contact your account team.

Investigating matching requests

When a managed or custom response rule logs or blocks a transaction, the event is available in Security Events. This means responders can trace any detection back to the full context of the request and the specific rule that took action.

At the moment, both request-only rules and full-transaction rules are shown together in the same analytics page. In Security Events, the events generated by response rules are part of the Managed Rules or Custom Rules service. You can filter events belonging to a specific rule ID in the relative rule list section.

Get started today

Full transaction detection is generally available for all zones proxying traffic through Cloudflare. To verify that you’re protected, go to Security > Security Rules in the Cloudflare dashboard. If you want to customize your policy, start by reviewing full transaction detections in Security Analytics, then create the response phase policy that fits your application.
